chains.title: A copper supply disruption and the cost of grids and buildings
chains.disruption: Output falls at mines or refineries in a leading producing country, through outages, lower ore grades or policy.

links.text: Largest named producer of 2025 world mine output
Largest named producer of 2025 world refinery output
A recorded disruption, in USGS's words
Electricity networks' part of copper demand from energy technologies, IEA 2025
Copper's US end uses, as USGS cites them
One US fabricator on passing raw-material costs to customers
If refined copper becomes scarcer, cable, transformer and building-wire costs would rise, and projects with fixed budgets could be delayed or rescoped.
Any effect on inflation or growth would depend on how large and lasting the disruption is; this page does not measure it.

indirect: Utilities and their customers, through network costs
Electric vehicle and electrical equipment makers

gains_losses.who: Copper producers outside the disrupted region
gains_losses.mechanism: Higher prices on output that is not disrupted.
Scrap is worth more when refined copper costs more.

gains_losses.who: Fabricators that cannot pass costs through quickly
gains_losses.mechanism: Margins narrow between raw-material cost and product prices until prices adjust.

gains_losses.who: Builders and grid contractors on fixed-price contracts
gains_losses.mechanism: Input costs rise while contract revenue does not.

mitigants: Aluminum substitution in cable, radiators and tubing, which USGS names
Stocks or spare refining capacity elsewhere
chains.learned: Measured here: the largest named producers of copper mine and refinery output, and the IEA's split of energy-technology demand. Stated by sources in this chain: a recorded disruption, US end uses and one fabricator's cost pass-through.
chains.assumed: Not measured here: price responses, project delays, and any effect on inflation or growth.

chains.title: Cobalt export restrictions and battery supply
chains.disruption: The leading producing country restricts or halts cobalt exports.

links.text: Largest named producer of 2025 world mine output
Concentration of 2025 world mine output (HHI bounds)
Electric vehicles' part of cobalt demand from energy technologies, IEA 2025
US net import reliance, 2025, as USGS prints it
A cut in exports from the leading country would reduce the cobalt available to refiners and battery makers elsewhere.
Battery makers could shift to chemistries that use less or no cobalt, or secure supply from other countries; both take time.

gains_losses.mechanism: Higher prices for supply that is not restricted.

gains_losses.who: Makers of low-cobalt or cobalt-free battery chemistries
gains_losses.mechanism: Demand moves toward chemistries less exposed to the restriction.

gains_losses.who: Battery makers tied to cobalt-rich chemistries
gains_losses.mechanism: Higher input costs and less certain supply.

mitigants: Stocks held by refiners and users
chains.learned: Measured here: how concentrated cobalt mining is, the IEA's share of electric vehicles in energy-technology demand, and US reliance as printed.
chains.assumed: Not measured here: any restriction itself, price effects, and how fast battery makers can change chemistry.

chains.title: A lithium supply shortfall and battery costs
chains.disruption: Lithium mining or refining falls short of battery makers' needs.

links.text: Largest named producer of 2025 world mine output
Largest named holder of 2025 world reserves
Years of reserves at the 2025 rate (not a depletion date)
Electric vehicles' part of lithium demand from energy technologies, IEA 2025
A shortfall would raise battery-cell costs or slow deliveries to electric vehicle and storage makers.
Reserves large relative to output allow supply to grow over time, but new mines and refineries take years to build.

indirect: Electricity customers where storage is planned

gains_losses.who: Lithium producers with spare or new capacity
gains_losses.mechanism: Higher prices while supply is short.

gains_losses.who: Battery and vehicle makers without secured supply
gains_losses.mechanism: Higher input costs or delayed production.

mitigants: Chemistries that use lithium more efficiently
chains.learned: Measured here, where USGS names the order: who leads mining and reserves, years of reserves at the 2025 rate, and the IEA's share of electric vehicles in energy-technology demand.
chains.assumed: Not measured here: whether a shortfall occurs, its size, and price or delivery effects.

chains.title: Rare earth export limits and permanent magnets
chains.disruption: The leading producing country limits exports of rare earths or of the magnets made from them.

links.text: Largest named producer of 2025 world mine output
Wind's part of neodymium demand from energy technologies, IEA 2025
Electric vehicles' part of neodymium demand from energy technologies, IEA 2025
Export limits would reduce the magnet materials available to motor, turbine and equipment makers elsewhere.
Makers could redesign motors to use fewer rare earths or build supply in other countries; both take time.

gains_losses.who: Rare earth miners and processors in other countries
gains_losses.mechanism: Demand turns to supply outside the restricting country.

gains_losses.who: Makers that depend on imported magnets

mitigants: Motor designs using fewer rare earths
chains.learned: Measured here: the largest named producer of rare earth mine output, and the parts of neodymium's energy-technology demand that go to wind and to electric vehicles, as the IEA splits it.
chains.assumed: Not measured here: any export limit itself, magnet supply, and the time redesign takes.

chains.title: Policy change in the leading nickel producer
chains.disruption: The leading producing country changes its rules on mining, processing or exports.

links.text: Largest named producer of 2025 world mine output
Concentration of 2025 world mine output (HHI bounds)
Electric vehicles' part of nickel demand from energy technologies, IEA 2025
US net import reliance, 2025, as USGS prints it
A change in the leading country's rules could shift where nickel is processed and what it costs users elsewhere.

indirect: Construction and appliance makers using stainless steel

gains_losses.mechanism: Rules that favour local processing move work to them.

gains_losses.who: Processors elsewhere that depend on its ore

mitigants: Recycling of stainless steel and batteries
chains.learned: Measured here: how concentrated nickel mining is, the IEA's share of electric vehicles in energy-technology demand, and US reliance as printed.
chains.assumed: Not measured here: any rule change, and its effect on prices or processing.

chains.title: Curbs on aluminum smelting in the leading producer
chains.disruption: Smelting output falls in the leading producing country, for example through power limits or policy.

links.text: Largest named producer of 2025 world smelter output
Concentration of 2025 world smelter output (HHI bounds)
US net import reliance, 2025, as USGS prints it
Smelting uses a great deal of electricity, so power costs or limits in the leading country could change world supply.
Less smelter output would raise costs for packaging, transport, construction and power-line makers that use aluminum.

gains_losses.who: Smelters in other countries with available power
gains_losses.mechanism: Higher prices for metal that is not curtailed.

chains.learned: Measured here: how concentrated smelting is and US reliance as printed.
chains.assumed: Not measured here: power conditions, any curb, and price effects. The electricity intensity of smelting is general knowledge, not from a retained source.
